newsitem.title: GERMANY: German experts defend EU gene-soya approval.
newsitem.headline: German experts defend EU gene-soya approval.

text.p: German academics on Thursday defended as sound a European Union decision earlier this year to allow the marketing of products derived from genetically altered U.S. soybeans.
And a Bonn farm ministry official said EU law did not allow any discrimination against the products.
The experts were addressing an audience at the EuroTier livestock industry exhibition here.
"Soy oil from genetically modified soybeans is completely identical to oil made from conventional beans," said Kristiane Sinemus of the institute for biochemistry at Darmstadt University.
Any live genetic organisms would be killed in the various stages of processing beans into oil, which included heat treatment at 106 and 220 degrees, she said.
Environmentalist groups are concerned that U.S. chemicals firm Monsanto's new soybean, which is mixed in with bean shipments to the EU for crushing, could be a threat to health.
The beans, modified to resist the company's herbicide Round Up, form two percent of this year's U.S. soybean crop.
Gerhard Jahreis, a food and environment specialist at Jena University, said U.S. animal tests showed soymeal from Monsanto's beans had the same properties as those from traditonal ones.
"There were no substantial differences in nutrition, composition and feed value," he said.
But he told Reuters the experiments had been done and publicised under time pressure and should be followed up by research into long-term feeding effects in Germany.
"I'd like to look into what happens in animals' digestive systems when they are fed this soymeal for some time, I've put together a project plan but haven't found funding," he said.

Uwe Petersen of the German farm ministry said national and EU feeds law did not provide for labelling of soymeal derived from the new soybeans -- a key demand of the protestors -- but the industry could choose to do so voluntarily.
Similarly, the food industry was free to reveal on labels whether its products contained soy oil from the new beans.
"But these labelling decisions would be a question of the assumed, rather than actual, qualities of the product," he said.
